A default constructor is a member function that requires no parameters when called, is named after the type it constructs, and can use a member initializer list to initialize members and a constructor body for more complex setup. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 240]

Constructors are called when an object is created, such as when instantiating automatic variables, creating arrays, or allocating memory with new. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 240] [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 242]

A destructor is a function without arguments, named after its type with a tilde prefix, that is called when a user-defined object is about to be destroyed. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 242]

When an object is destroyed, its destructor cleans up resources (such as freeing dynamically allocated memory via delete[]), and child destructors automatically invoke their base class destructors and member destructors. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 242]

Constructors and destructors can also manage resource lifecycles automatically as part of RAII, where a constructor acquires a resource (such as locking a mutex) and the guaranteed destructor call releases it (such as unlocking the mutex). [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 469]
